questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose the US as I wanted to have a completely new cultural experience. The whole college life is so different from studying in Copenhagen. Of course, it would have still been fun to do an exchange in another European city, but I wouldn’t be that different from the school system I’m already used to. I really liked the idea of living on campus and having a large amount of school engagement.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some of the most fun I have had in a long time. I met a lot of incredible people right from the beginning and stayed friends with them till the end. Even went traveling multiple times to Miami, New York, New Orleans and Nashville with the other exchange students throughout the semester and at the end of our stay.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: They send out a lot of information beforehand and the study aboard office was always available to help with any questions. It definitely was confusing, but you always had someone to ask, either employees from the university or fellow students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The school held a two day orientation and social event on the first day, that covert most of the important information, plus it gave you a network of other exchange students so you weren’t alone in figuring out the practical details. The questions I had, I just asked them physically during the orientation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You could either get a dorm room or a room in a student apartment that you shared with four other roommates. I chose to stay in the global village dorm room that was recommended by the university to exchange students, so we were a lot of people staying in the same building that was located very central on main campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
As I stayed in a dorm room the kitchen facilities weren’t great, they did have a kitchen in the building, but you had to buy all your own utensils and everything, so I didn’t feel worth it when only staying for the semester. Me and my friends all had the 120-block + 500 dining dollars meal plan which consisted of 120 meal swipes that counted as a entry to one of the dining halls on campus where you could get as much as you wanted buffet style. The 500 dining dollars are just dollars on your student card that you could use on all the on-campus food and café places. So, you would be able to buy coffee, takeaway, ice creme and whatever. I bought yoghurt and oatmeal for breakfast from the supermarket so I could just eat it in my dorm room. 
It was also possible to get a unlimited meal plan with all the meal swipes you want, but honestly wouldn’t have been worth it, because you are not going to go to the dining hall three times a day, trust me.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I definitely think living on campus is the better option as you are close to everything, and you will properly end up living right next to dome of your friends. My 3 best friends from the exchange all lived in the same building, so we would just do everything together, like eat dinner, study, go to the gym and so on. If you are a person who really needs to be alone and have their personal space the student apartments are also a good option, but you will not live as central, compared to global village where everything is within walking distance. 
I think for me the most important thing was to live in the center with other exchange students so I would get the most out of my stay. I defiantly missed having my own room, but it’s only a semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Let's be real dorm rooms are not the nicest., but would still say it's worth it for the network

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I was a little hard to figure out their system. They had a very complex university system with lots of different sites and forms. It is the kind of thing that made a lot of sense when you got to know it, but the process till there was frustrating for sure.  
The study aboard office were very good at sending out emails about what forms you had to submit and where, so as long as you check your email often and trust that it is all going to work it self out they you’ll be fine.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The study abord office was very fast to respond on email, so do not hesitate to just ask, that’s what they are there for.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: You had to register for a lot of options for classes, so you will get some of those. I was a little hard finding classes that were not too beginner level as my danish major did not exist in their school, so I didn’t have the right prequal for some of the classes.  One thing I learnt when I got there is that even though you are waitlisted for a class you want you always have the option to just show up to the fist class and ask if you can join, a lot of people will change classes in the first week so there is a big change of you getting the classes you want. I did this for one of my classes where my professor actually just texted the school to put me in the class because she thought it was interesting to have an exchange student with a different perspective.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Read all the emails and trust the process, everyone is trying to help you. And trust me it takes a long time and fustration.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think I had some very interesting classes, and your exchange is a good opportunity to try something different. That being said it is not a very high level compared to the danish university, a lot of the work just consist of remembering the material.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The classes have homework, exams during the semester and take attendance so you’ll need to stay engaged throughout the semester. But that also mean that the final exam does not count for everything, and you’ll manage your grade throughout the semester, so it’s not very stressful exam period which is really nice when you are on exchange and have a lot of other things you are doing.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to biological anthropology
Introduction to cultural anthropology
Introduction to persuasion theory
Relational communication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Relational communication is the best class I have ever taken. It is basically dating 101, but at university. The teacher was the nicest person, and would bake cookie for the class and would use my perspective for a lot of the class discussions.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You will spend a lot of money on traveling, so be prepared for that. Of course this is not necessary, but so worth it to see some other places while you are there.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Meal plans on campus were quite expensive

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of the athletic clubs were very high level or needed a lot of engagement. It’s not like lest meet ones a week and play volleyball, they are 4 times a week plus weekend trips.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They had all kinds of club and events all the time, you just had to look around, then you would be able to find whatever. The biggest event was football games, where you would meet a couple of hours before outside the stadium and do tailgating, which is basically just drinking in the parking lot. I don’t even like football but everyone went so it was a  lot of fun (only in the fall semester)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They had a free gym on campus 1 min from my housing. The nicest gym I have ever been to. It was so big and had literally everything. Of course, all the normal gym stuff, but then you could also play badminton, tennis, racquet ball, go bouldering, or swimming. Additionally, they had a lot of fitness classes for free, so you could do Pilates, yoga, spinning etc. All the exchange students used to the gym so much as a hang out spot, me and my friends took so many classes, just to try different things and as a fun activity. My favorite was the line dancing class we took ones a week, seriously the most fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I went on a lot of trips with my exchange student friends. We went on a round trip to the mountain and Nashville, a weekend trip to New Orleans, fall break in New York, and ended my semester by going with a friend to Miami and Key West in Florida. A lot of people also went to the coast like Outer Banks and Charlston, which looked so nice, but I didn’t have time. It is a bit hard traveling around the places nearby actually because you need a car, so you either have to rent one or get some good American friends. 
New Orleans was my favorite trip, such a recommendation. Good food, fun nightlife and lots of alligators in the swamp. Stay at Hi Hostel if you want to meet other people.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I was pretty easy for me. But I’ve traveled a lot and been on high school exchange in Argentina before, so I’m used to adjusting to new cultures. But the American people are pretty open, so any doubts you can just ask.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I was somewhat hard to make good American friends for me, as the people in my class were a bit younger than I was. But Americans really like socializing so if you meet someone, don’t be afraid to ask them if they want to hang out and introduce you to some of their friends. Not sure this is the best advice, but I started dating an American ended up spending a lot of time with his friend group as well. So basically, just take the opportunities you have to meet new people. I know a lot of exchange students got American friends if they were involved in clubs or if they had American roommates.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I think I’m used to the danish culture of being more nonchalant, so you have to get used to the American way of being overly excited about everything or always be very polite.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They are very open, they really do want to talk to you, and think it’s interesting that you are an exchange student

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Engage yourself in the experience. Try all the things available while you are there, you can always chill and watch Netflix when you get back home. So whatever people invite you for just say yes. And don’t spend too much time talking to people at home, trust me they will still be your friends when you get back, it is honestly a waste of time, and distances you from the experience you are having.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Live on-campus and spend time on campus. And save money to travel.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: You gain such a good network very quickly. I met the people I ended up hanging out with everyday during the orientation, and then we just hung out ever since. No one has a local network so everyone is down to just hang out all the time, and even go traveling together with people that you have known for a couple of weeks.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Honestly, I was chilling. The only challenging part was the whole process before with visa, housing and registration. Ones you’re there it’s just cool.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go alone! don't go with a friend. The idea is nice, but you are making it much harder for yourself to make good friends, and you’ll be stuck with them for the whole semester. All the people who did not go with anyone they new beforehand got a closer friend group a lot quicker, and became better friends with the people.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
